lesson.title: Four Steps to a Trustworthy Simulation
lesson.summary: A well built simulation follows a deliberate sequence: state the correspondence between the chance model and the real probabilities, define one trial and what counts as a success, run many trials, then state a conclusion in context.
lesson.body:
Simulation is powerful, but only if it is built carefully, since a sloppy chance model gives you a confident sounding number that has nothing to do with the real situation. A trustworthy simulation follows four steps. State: describe the real world probabilities and set up a random device, such as digits, coins, or dice, whose own probabilities match them exactly. Simulate one trial: define precisely what sequence of random outcomes makes up a single trial, and what result counts as a "success" for the question being asked. Do many trials: repeat the one trial procedure a large number of times, recording the outcome each time. Conclude: use the proportion of successes across all trials as your estimate, stated in the context of the original question.

Here is a worked example that carries the process through concretely. A basketball player makes each free throw independently with probability 0.7. You want to estimate the probability she makes at least 8 of her next 10 shots.

State: each shot is independent with P(make) equal to 0.7. Assign single random digits so that exactly 7 out of the 10 digits represent a make, matching 0.7 exactly: let digits 0 through 6 mean "make" and digits 7, 8, and 9 mean "miss."

Simulate one trial: a trial is a string of 10 random digits, one digit per shot. Count how many of the 10 digits fall in the 0 through 6 range. If that count is 8, 9, or 10, the trial is a success; otherwise it is a failure. Here is what one trial looks like using the digit string 3, 8, 1, 4, 9, 0, 6, 2, 7, 5. Classify each digit: 3 make, 8 miss, 1 make, 4 make, 9 miss, 0 make, 6 make, 2 make, 7 miss, 5 make. That comes out to 7 makes and 3 misses. Since 7 is not at least 8, this particular trial is recorded as a failure.

Do many trials: repeat this digit by digit process a large number of times, ideally 50 or more, using a calculator, computer, or a random digit table to generate the digit strings quickly.

Conclude: count how many of the trials were successes, divide by the total number of trials, and that proportion is your estimate of the probability of making at least 8 of 10 shots. A single trial like the one worked out above tells you almost nothing by itself, which is exactly why the "do many trials" step exists, and why the next section looks at random digit tables as a fast, reliable source of the digits a simulation like this one needs.
